claim: Wingless (Wg)/Wnt signaling is conserved in all metazoan animals.
source: Wingless (Wg)/Wnt signaling is conserved in all metazoan animals and plays critical roles in development.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the conservation of Wg/Wnt signaling across metazoan animals.

claim: Wingless (Wg)/Wnt signaling plays critical roles in development.
source: Wingless (Wg)/Wnt signaling is conserved in all metazoan animals and plays critical roles in development.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the role of Wg/Wnt signaling in development.

claim: The Wg/Wnt morphogen reception is essential for signal activation.
source: The Wg/Wnt morphogen reception is essential for signal activation, whose activity is mediated through the receptor complex and a scaffold protein Dishevelled (Dsh).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the requirement of morphogen reception for signal activation.

claim: Wg/Wnt morphogen reception activity is mediated through the receptor complex and a scaffold protein Dishevelled (Dsh).
source: The Wg/Wnt morphogen reception is essential for signal activation, whose activity is mediated through the receptor complex and a scaffold protein Dishevelled (Dsh).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the molecular mediators of Wg/Wnt signaling.

claim: The exon junction complex (EJC) activity is indispensable for Wg signaling by maintaining an appropriate level of Dsh protein for Wg ligand reception in Drosophila.
source: We report here that the exon junction complex (EJC) activity is indispensable for Wg signaling by maintaining an appropriate level of Dsh protein for Wg ligand reception in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The EJC controls the splicing of the cell polarity gene discs large 1 (dlg1) in Drosophila wing imaginal discs.
source: Transcriptome analyses in Drosophila wing imaginal discs indicate that the EJC controls the splicing of the cell polarity gene discs large 1 (dlg1), whose coding protein directly interacts with Dsh.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analyses (RNA-seq data) presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dlg1 protein directly interacts with Dsh.
source: Transcriptome analyses in Drosophila wing imaginal discs indicate that the EJC controls the splicing of the cell polarity gene discs large 1 (dlg1), whose coding protein directly interacts with Dsh.
evidence: This is supported by biochemical experiments (co-immunoprecipitation) shown in the manuscript.

claim: Dlg1 protein acts independently from its role in cell polarity to protect Dsh protein from lysosomal degradation.
source: Genetic and biochemical experiments demonstrate that Dlg1 protein acts independently from its role in cell polarity to protect Dsh protein from lysosomal degradation.
evidence: This is supported by genetic and biochemical experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human orthologous Dlg protein is sufficient to promote Dvl protein stabilization.
source: More importantly, human orthologous Dlg protein is sufficient to promote Dvl protein stabilization and Wnt signaling activity, thus revealing a conserved regulatory mechanism of Wg/Wnt signaling by Dlg and EJC.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in human cells presented in the manuscript.

claim: Human orthologous Dlg protein is sufficient to promote Wnt signaling activity.
source: More importantly, human orthologous Dlg protein is sufficient to promote Dvl protein stabilization and Wnt signaling activity, thus revealing a conserved regulatory mechanism of Wg/Wnt signaling by Dlg and EJC.
evidence: This is supported by TOPFlash reporter assays in human cells presented in the manuscript.

claim: The regulatory mechanism of Wg/Wnt signaling by Dlg and EJC is conserved.
source: More importantly, human orthologous Dlg protein is sufficient to promote Dvl protein stabilization and Wnt signaling activity, thus revealing a conserved regulatory mechanism of Wg/Wnt signaling by Dlg and EJC.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both Drosophila and human systems show similar regulatory patterns.

claim: Dysregulation of Wg/Wnt signaling in humans results in developmental defects.
source: Given the importance of Wg/Wnt signaling in many cellular processes, it is not surprising that dysregulation of Wg/Wnt signaling in humans results in developmental defects as well as cancer (MacDonald et al., 2009; Clevers and Nusse, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of Wg/Wnt signaling in humans results in cancer.
source: Given the importance of Wg/Wnt signaling in many cellular processes, it is not surprising that dysregulation of Wg/Wnt signaling in humans results in developmental defects as well as cancer (MacDonald et al., 2009; Clevers and Nusse, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila, Wg ligand binds to the seven-pass transmembrane receptors Frizzled/Frizzled2 (Fz/Fz2).
source: In Drosophila, Wg ligand binds to the seven-pass transmembrane receptors Frizzled/Frizzled2 (Fz/Fz2) and a co-receptor Arrow (Arr), a homolog of vertebrate LRP5/6.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Wg signaling components.

claim: In Drosophila, Wg ligand binds to a co-receptor Arrow (Arr).
source: In Drosophila, Wg ligand binds to the seven-pass transmembrane receptors Frizzled/Frizzled2 (Fz/Fz2) and a co-receptor Arrow (Arr), a homolog of vertebrate LRP5/6.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Wg signaling components.

claim: Arrow (Arr) is a homolog of vertebrate LRP5/6.
source: In Drosophila, Wg ligand binds to the seven-pass transmembrane receptors Frizzled/Frizzled2 (Fz/Fz2) and a co-receptor Arrow (Arr), a homolog of vertebrate LRP5/6.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about protein homology.

claim: Formation of the Wg-Fz/Fz2-Arr trimeric complex activates Dishevelled (Dsh) on the plasma membrane.
source: Formation of this trimeric complex activates a scaffold protein Dishevelled (Dsh) on the plasma membrane, leading to disruption of the Axin-mediated degradation complex and hence stabilization of Armadillo (Arm), a homolog of vertebrate β-catenin.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Wg signaling mechanism.

claim: Activation of Dishevelled (Dsh) leads to disruption of the Axin-mediated degradation complex.
source: Formation of this trimeric complex activates a scaffold protein Dishevelled (Dsh) on the plasma membrane, leading to disruption of the Axin-mediated degradation complex and hence stabilization of Armadillo (Arm), a homolog of vertebrate β-catenin.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Wg signaling mechanism.

claim: Disruption of the Axin-mediated degradation complex leads to stabilization of Armadillo (Arm).
source: Formation of this trimeric complex activates a scaffold protein Dishevelled (Dsh) on the plasma membrane, leading to disruption of the Axin-mediated degradation complex and hence stabilization of Armadillo (Arm), a homolog of vertebrate β-catenin.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about Wg signaling mechanism.

claim: Armadillo (Arm) is a homolog of vertebrate β-catenin.
source: Formation of this trimeric complex activates a scaffold protein Dishevelled (Dsh) on the plasma membrane, leading to disruption of the Axin-mediated degradation complex and hence stabilization of Armadillo (Arm), a homolog of vertebrate β-catenin.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about protein homology.

claim: Accumulated Arm translocates to the nucleus to activate target gene transcription.
source: Accumulated Arm then translocates to the nucleus to activate target gene transcription (MacDonald and He, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A genome-wide RNAi screen in the developing Drosophila wing identified the exon junction complex (EJC) as a positive regulator of Wg signaling.
source: To unveil novel regulators of Wg signaling, we conducted a genome-wide RNAi screen in the developing Drosophila wing, from which a RNA binding exon junction complex (EJC) emerged as a positive regulator of Wg signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi screen data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The EJC acts in several aspects of posttranscriptional regulation, including mRNA localization, translation and degradation.
source: The EJC is known to act in several aspects of posttranscriptional regulation, including mRNA localization, translation and degradation (Tange et al., 2004; Le Hir et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: After transcription, the pre-mRNA associated subunit eIF4AIII is loaded to nascent transcripts about 20–24 bases upstream of each exon junction.
source: After transcription, the pre-mRNA associated subunit eIF4AIII is loaded to nascent transcripts about 20–24 bases upstream of each exon junction, resulting in binding of Mago nashi (Mago)/Magoh and Tsunagi (Tsu)/Y14 proteins to form the pre-EJC core complex.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about EJC assembly.

claim: Loading of eIF4AIII to nascent transcripts results in binding of Mago nashi (Mago)/Magoh and Tsunagi (Tsu)/Y14 proteins to form the pre-EJC core complex.
source: After transcription, the pre-mRNA associated subunit eIF4AIII is loaded to nascent transcripts about 20–24 bases upstream of each exon junction, resulting in binding of Mago nashi (Mago)/Magoh and Tsunagi (Tsu)/Y14 proteins to form the pre-EJC core complex.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about EJC assembly.

claim: The pre-EJC recruits other proteins including Barentsz (Btz) to facilitate its diverse function.
source: The pre-EJC then recruits other proteins including Barentsz (Btz) to facilitate its diverse function (Shibuya et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In vertebrates, the EJC ensures translation efficiency.
source: In vertebrates, the EJC is known to ensure translation efficiency (Nott et al., 2004) as well as to activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) (Gatfield et al., 2003; Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In vertebrates, the EJC activates nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD).
source: In vertebrates, the EJC is known to ensure translation efficiency (Nott et al., 2004) as well as to activate nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) (Gatfield et al., 2003; Chang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila, the EJC does not contribute to NMD.
source: In Drosophila, however, the EJC does not contribute to NMD (Gatfield et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila, the EJC is required for the oskar mRNA localization to the posterior pole of the oocyte.
source: It is instead required for the oskar mRNA localization to the posterior pole of the oocyte (Newmark and Boswell, 1994; Hachet and Ephrussi, 2001; Mohr et al., 2001; van Eeden et al., 2001; Palacios et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The pre-EJC plays an important role in alternative splicing of mRNA in Drosophila.
source: Very recently, the pre-EJC has been shown to play an important role in alternative splicing of mRNA in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a statement about recent findings in the field.

claim: Reduced EJC expression results in exon skipping in MAPK and transcripts that contain long introns or are located at heterochromatin.
source: Reduced EJC expression results in two forms of aberrant splicing. One is the exon skipping, which occurs in MAPK and transcripts that contain long introns or are located at heterochromatin (Ashton-Beaucage et al., 2010; Roignant and Treisman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reduced EJC expression results in intron retention on piwi transcripts.
source: The other is the intron retention on piwi transcripts (Hayashi et al., 2014; Malone et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The role of EJC in alternative splicing is conserved in vertebrates.
source: Furthermore, transcriptome analyses in cultured cells indicates the role of EJC in alternative splicing is also conserved in vertebrates (Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The pre-EJC positively regulates Wg signaling through its effect on facilitating Wg morphogen reception.
source: We find that the pre-EJC positively regulates Wg signaling through its effect on facilitating Wg morphogen reception.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The basolateral cell polarity gene discs large 1 (dlg1) is an in vivo target of the pre-EJC in Wg signaling.
source: Further studies reveal that the basolateral cell polarity gene discs large 1 (dlg1) is an in vivo target of the pre-EJC in Wg signaling.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome and genetic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dlg1 acts independently from its role on cell polarity to stabilize Dsh protein.
source: We show that Dlg1 acts independently from its role on cell polarity to stabilize Dsh protein, thus allowing Wg protein internalization required for signaling activation.
evidence: This is supported by genetic and biochemical experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dlg1 stabilization of Dsh protein allows Wg protein internalization required for signaling activation.
source: We show that Dlg1 acts independently from its role on cell polarity to stabilize Dsh protein, thus allowing Wg protein internalization required for signaling activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that Dlg1 stabilizes Dsh and that Wg accumulates extracellularly when Dlg1 is absent.

claim: Human Dlg2 exhibits a protective role on Dvl proteins to enhance Wnt signaling in cultured human cells.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrate that human Dlg2 exhibits a similar protective role on Dvl proteins to enhance Wnt signaling in cultured human cells.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in HEK293T cells presented in the manuscript.

claim: Knocking down tsu, mago, or eIF4AIII resulted in loss of marginal tissues and sensory bristles in adult Drosophila wing blade.
source: In an in vivo RNAi screen, we found that knocking down three core components of the pre-EJC, tsu, mago and eIF4AIII, respectively, resulted in loss of marginal tissues and sensory bristles in adult Drosophila wing blade (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G), which resembles stereotypical phenotypes associated with reduced Wg signaling.
evidence: This is supported by the RNAi screen data and images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G.

claim: Loss of marginal tissues and sensory bristles in adult Drosophila wing blade resembles stereotypical phenotypes associated with reduced Wg signaling.
source: In an in vivo RNAi screen, we found that knocking down three core components of the pre-EJC, tsu, mago and eIF4AIII, respectively, resulted in loss of marginal tissues and sensory bristles in adult Drosophila wing blade (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–G), which resembles stereotypical phenotypes associated with reduced Wg signaling.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Wg signaling phenotypes.

claim: Loss-of-function tsuΔ18 mutants displayed defects in wing development.
source: Furthermore, loss-of-function tsuΔ18 or mago93D mutants (Roignant and Treisman, 2010) displayed similar defects in wing development (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the phenotypic data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Loss-of-function mago93D mutants displayed defects in wing development.
source: Furthermore, loss-of-function tsuΔ18 or mago93D mutants (Roignant and Treisman, 2010) displayed similar defects in wing development (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the phenotypic data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Sens protein production is lost in tsu somatic clones in wing imaginal discs.
source: We observed obvious loss of Sens and Dll protein production in tsu or mago somatic clones (Figure 1C–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Dll protein production is lost in tsu somatic clones in wing imaginal discs.
source: We observed obvious loss of Sens and Dll protein production in tsu or mago somatic clones (Figure 1C–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1E,F.

claim: Sens protein production is lost in mago somatic clones in wing imaginal discs.
source: We observed obvious loss of Sens and Dll protein production in tsu or mago somatic clones (Figure 1C–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Dll protein production is lost in mago somatic clones in wing imaginal discs.
source: We observed obvious loss of Sens and Dll protein production in tsu or mago somatic clones (Figure 1C–F; Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Sens expression was not altered in somatic clones of btz.
source: However, Sens expression was not altered in somatic clones of btz (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B), which is a cytoplasmic component of the EJC (Palacios et al., 2004), suggesting that the role of EJC in Wg signaling is independent of its cytoplasmic function.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Btz is a cytoplasmic component of the EJC.
source: However, Sens expression was not altered in somatic clones of btz (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B), which is a cytoplasmic component of the EJC (Palacios et al., 2004), suggesting that the role of EJC in Wg signaling is independent of its cytoplasmic function.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The role of EJC in Wg signaling is independent of its cytoplasmic function.
source: However, Sens expression was not altered in somatic clones of btz (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B), which is a cytoplasmic component of the EJC (Palacios et al., 2004), suggesting that the role of EJC in Wg signaling is independent of its cytoplasmic function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that btz loss does not affect Wg signaling while other EJC components do.

claim: The expression of fz3-lacZ was decreased when tsu activity was reduced.
source: As expected, the expression of fz3-lacZ and Dll-lacZ was decreased when tsu activity was reduced (Figure 1G,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: This is supported by lacZ reporter data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The expression of Dll-lacZ was decreased when tsu activity was reduced.
source: As expected, the expression of fz3-lacZ and Dll-lacZ was decreased when tsu activity was reduced (Figure 1G,H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: This is supported by lacZ reporter data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–J.

claim: The amount of Wg protein present in tsu mutant clones was significantly increased.
source: We found that the amount of Wg protein present in tsu or mago, but not btz, mutant clones was significantly increased (Figure 2A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A–C.

claim: The amount of Wg protein present in mago mutant clones was significantly increased.
source: We found that the amount of Wg protein present in tsu or mago, but not btz, mutant clones was significantly increased (Figure 2A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F.

claim: The amount of Wg protein present in btz mutant clones was not increased.
source: We found that the amount of Wg protein present in tsu or mago, but not btz, mutant clones was significantly increased (Figure 2A–C; Figure 1—figure supplement 2E,F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: Wg signaling was ectopically activated in wildtype cells immediately next to tsu mutant clones.
source: Clue to the understanding of this apparent contradiction came from the observation that Wg signaling was ectopically activated in wildtype cells immediately next to mutant clones (insets of Figures 1D and 2C).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in insets of Figures 1D and 2C.

claim: Increased Wg protein present in mutant clones is sufficient to activate signaling in neighboring wildtype cells.
source: This result suggests that increased Wg protein present in mutant clones is sufficient to activate signaling in neighboring wildtype cells whilst mutant cells are incapable of receiving Wg input.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of ectopic Wg signaling activation in cells adjacent to mutant clones.

claim: Mutant cells are incapable of receiving Wg input.
source: This result suggests that increased Wg protein present in mutant clones is sufficient to activate signaling in neighboring wildtype cells whilst mutant cells are incapable of receiving Wg input.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Wg accumulates in mutant cells but signaling is not activated within them.

claim: The Wg signaling defects observed in mutant cells are caused by blockage of Wg reception at the plasma membrane.
source: Therefore, the Wg signaling defects observed in mutant cells could be caused by blockage of Wg reception at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Wg accumulation and lack of signaling in mutant cells.

claim: Extracellular Wg protein accumulated significantly in both apical and basolateral extracellular spaces in tsu mutant clones.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, extracellular Wg protein (Strigini and Cohen, 2000) accumulated significantly in both apical and basolateral extracellular spaces (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular Wg staining data shown in Figure 2D–F.

claim: The increased extracellular Wg was not due to heightened wg gene transcription.
source: Furthermore, we showed that the increased extracellular Wg was not due to heightened wg gene transcription nor Wg protein secretion in producing cells because neither the expression of wg-lacZ (a wg transcription reporter) nor the amount of NRT-Wg (a membrane-tethered form of Wg) was altered (Figure 2G–K; also see Figure 3—figure supplement 3B for wg transcription analyses).
evidence: This is supported by wg-lacZ reporter data shown in Figure 2G–I and transcription analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The increased extracellular Wg was not due to increased Wg protein secretion in producing cells.
source: Furthermore, we showed that the increased extracellular Wg was not due to heightened wg gene transcription nor Wg protein secretion in producing cells because neither the expression of wg-lacZ (a wg transcription reporter) nor the amount of NRT-Wg (a membrane-tethered form of Wg) was altered (Figure 2G–K; also see Figure 3—figure supplement 3B for wg transcription analyses).
evidence: This is supported by NRT-Wg data shown in Figure 2J,K.

claim: Inhibiting Wg protein endocytosis by reducing the activity of Wg receptor complex Fz2/Arr results in accumulation of Wg protein on the plasma membrane.
source: Previous studies have shown that inhibiting Wg protein endocytosis by reducing either the activity of Wg receptor complex Fz2/Arr or the scaffold protein Dsh results in accumulation of Wg protein on the plasma membrane (Han et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Inhibiting Wg protein endocytosis by reducing the activity of the scaffold protein Dsh results in accumulation of Wg protein on the plasma membrane.
source: Previous studies have shown that inhibiting Wg protein endocytosis by reducing either the activity of Wg receptor complex Fz2/Arr or the scaffold protein Dsh results in accumulation of Wg protein on the plasma membrane (Han et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The expression of Dsh was obviously reduced in tsu mutant clones.
source: In tsu and mago mutant clones, we found that the expression of Dsh (Figure 3A–D), but not Fz2 or Arr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), was obviously reduced.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The expression of Dsh was obviously reduced in mago mutant clones.
source: In tsu and mago mutant clones, we found that the expression of Dsh (Figure 3A–D), but not Fz2 or Arr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), was obviously reduced.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: The expression of Fz2 was not reduced in tsu and mago mutant clones.
source: In tsu and mago mutant clones, we found that the expression of Dsh (Figure 3A–D), but not Fz2 or Arr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), was obviously reduced.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The expression of Arr was not reduced in tsu and mago mutant clones.
source: In tsu and mago mutant clones, we found that the expression of Dsh (Figure 3A–D), but not Fz2 or Arr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), was obviously reduced.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dsh protein production was reduced when tsu was knocked down by RNAi in S2 cells.
source: This result was further verified in cultured Drosophila Schneider 2 (S2) cells in which tsu or mago was knocked down by RNAi (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Dsh protein production was reduced when mago was knocked down by RNAi in S2 cells.
source: This result was further verified in cultured Drosophila Schneider 2 (S2) cells in which tsu or mago was knocked down by RNAi (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Overexpressed dsh was able to rescue the wing margin defects caused by tsu knockdown.
source: To unveil the functional importance of the EJC regulation on Dsh, overexpressed dsh was able to rescue the wing margin defects caused by tsu knockdown (Figure 3H; cf. Figure 3E), whereas fz2 or arr had little effect (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Overexpressed fz2 had little effect on rescuing the wing margin defects caused by tsu knockdown.
source: To unveil the functional importance of the EJC regulation on Dsh, overexpressed dsh was able to rescue the wing margin defects caused by tsu knockdown (Figure 3H; cf. Figure 3E), whereas fz2 or arr had little effect (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Overexpressed arr had little effect on rescuing the wing margin defects caused by tsu knockdown.
source: To unveil the functional importance of the EJC regulation on Dsh, overexpressed dsh was able to rescue the wing margin defects caused by tsu knockdown (Figure 3H; cf. Figure 3E), whereas fz2 or arr had little effect (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: This is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The pre-EJC acts primarily through Dsh in wing discs to regulate Wg signaling reception.
source: The above experiments suggest that the pre-EJC acts primarily through Dsh in wing discs to regulate Wg signaling reception.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments and the observation that Dsh levels are reduced in EJC mutants.

claim: The abundance of dlg1 mRNA was reduced when tsu dsRNA was expressed in wing discs.
source: Real time RT-PCR revealed that the abundance of dlg1, RhoGEF2 and l(2)gl, but not dsh mRNA, was reduced when tsu dsRNA was expressed in wing discs.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The abundance of RhoGEF2 mRNA was reduced when tsu dsRNA was expressed in wing discs.
source: Real time RT-PCR revealed that the abundance of dlg1, RhoGEF2 and l(2)gl, but not dsh mRNA, was reduced when tsu dsRNA was expressed in wing discs.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The abundance of l(2)gl mRNA was reduced when tsu dsRNA was expressed in wing discs.
source: Real time RT-PCR revealed that the abundance of dlg1, RhoGEF2 and l(2)gl, but not dsh mRNA, was reduced when tsu dsRNA was expressed in wing discs.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The abundance of dsh mRNA was not reduced when tsu dsRNA was expressed in wing discs.
source: Real time RT-PCR revealed that the abundance of dlg1, RhoGEF2 and l(2)gl, but not dsh mRNA, was reduced when tsu dsRNA was expressed in wing discs.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: The expression of 1447 mRNAs was altered by more than 25% when the pre-EJC activity was downregulated.
source: We found that the expression of 1447 mRNAs was altered by more than 25% when the pre-EJC activity was downregulated (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: 629 genes were identified whose expression was increased when the pre-EJC activity was downregulated.
source: This list likely includes both direct as well as indirect pre-EJC targets as 629 genes were identified whose expression was increased.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The expression of sens mRNA was decreased by more than 50% in wing discs expressing tsu RNAi.
source: Among those genes whose mRNA levels were reduced we found that the expression of sens and Dll mRNA, two Wg signaling transcription targets, was decreased by more than 50% in wing discs expressing tsu RNAi.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The expression of Dll mRNA was decreased by more than 50% in wing discs expressing tsu RNAi.
source: Among those genes whose mRNA levels were reduced we found that the expression of sens and Dll mRNA, two Wg signaling transcription targets, was decreased by more than 50% in wing discs expressing tsu RNAi.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: wg mRNA did not show an obvious change in wing discs expressing tsu RNAi.
source: Consistent with the RT-PCR result (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), wg and dsh mRNA did not show an obvious change.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: dsh mRNA did not show an obvious change in wing discs expressing tsu RNAi.
source: Consistent with the RT-PCR result (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), wg and dsh mRNA did not show an obvious change.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Among 818 mRNAs whose expression was downregulated, three genes (dlg1, l(2)gl, and dbo) encode proteins that directly interact with Dsh.
source: Among 818 mRNAs whose expression was downregulated, we identified three genes, dlg1, lethal (2) giant larvae [l(2)gl] and diablo (dbo), whose protein products are known to directly interact with Dsh.
evidence: This is based on comparison of RNA-seq data with annotated protein interaction information from FlyBase and literature.

claim: dlg1 was the candidate consistently exhibiting reduced expression in the pre-EJC-defective wing disc cells when compared with wildtype cells.
source: qPCR and RT-PCR analyses were then performed to confirm bona fide Dsh interactors that potentially mediate the pre-EJC activity on Dsh (Figure 3J; Figure 3—figure supplement 3B). In both cases, dlg1 was the candidate consistently exhibiting reduced expression in the pre-EJC-defective wing disc cells when compared with that in wildtype cells.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3J and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The amount of dlg1 mRNA was reduced by about 30% when the pre-EJC was dysfunctional.
source: These results fit well with RNA-seq analyses that the amount of dlg1 mRNA was reduced by about 30% when the pre-EJC was dysfunctional.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reduced dlg1 expression may be a consequence of altered RNA splicing.
source: We suspected that reduced dlg1 expression may be a consequence of altered RNA splicing.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known role of EJC in splicing.

claim: Exon inclusion is an aberrant splicing event caused by dysfunctional EJC.
source: Apart from previously reported exon skipping caused by dysfunctional EJC (Ashton-Beaucage et al., 2010; Roignant and Treisman, 2010), we uncovered two additional aberrant splicing events (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). The first event was exon inclusion, which retained exons that were normally efficiently spliced in specific isoforms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Exon inclusion likely increases the usage of splice sites.
source: This event likely increases the usage of splice sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of exon inclusion events.

claim: RNA-seq analyses revealed a slightly higher usage of annotated splice sites (1.4% higher usage for 5' splice sites and 1.5% for 3' splice sites) in pre-EJC depleted wing disc cells compared with wildtype cells.
source: Indeed the RNA-seq analyses revealed a slightly higher usage of annotated splice sites (i.e. 1.4% higher usage for 5' splice sites and 1.5% for 3' splice sites) in pre-EJC depleted wing disc cells compared with those in wildtype cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The second aberrant splicing event utilized previously unidentified splice sites to generate new introns and exons.
source: The second event utilized previously unidentified splice sites to generate new introns and exons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H, 2B,C; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and sequencing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F–H and Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: The pre-EJC plays a critical role in alternative splicing by preserving correct usage of splice sites to generate functional mRNA products.
source: Together, our bioinformatic analyses suggest that the pre-EJC plays a critical role in alternative splicing by preserving correct usage of splice sites to generate functional mRNA products.
evidence: This is inferred from the bioinformatic analyses of RNA-seq data.

claim: The amount of Dlg1 protein was reduced in tsu mutant wing disc clones.
source: The impact of the pre-EJC regulation on dlg1 splicing was further verified at the protein level as the amount of Dlg1 protein was reduced in tsu mutant wing disc clones (Figure 4A,B) as well as in S2 cells treated with dsRNA against individual components of the pre-EJC (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The amount of Dlg1 protein was reduced in S2 cells treated with dsRNA against individual components of the pre-EJC.
source: The impact of the pre-EJC regulation on dlg1 splicing was further verified at the protein level as the amount of Dlg1 protein was reduced in tsu mutant wing disc clones (Figure 4A,B) as well as in S2 cells treated with dsRNA against individual components of the pre-EJC (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The level of Dlg1 protein derived from a cDNA expression construct did not change when the pre-EJC was knocked down.
source: In contrast, the level of Dlg1 protein derived from a cDNA expression construct did not change (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Reduced dlg1 expression led to accumulation of extracellular Wg.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that reduced dlg1 expression led to accumulation of extracellular Wg (Figure 4C,D), attenuation of Wg signaling in wing discs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–D), and consequently loss of wing margin and sensory bristles in the adult wing blade (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by extracellular Wg staining data shown in Figure 4C,D.

claim: Reduced dlg1 expression led to attenuation of Wg signaling in wing discs.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that reduced dlg1 expression led to accumulation of extracellular Wg (Figure 4C,D), attenuation of Wg signaling in wing discs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–D), and consequently loss of wing margin and sensory bristles in the adult wing blade (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by Sens expression data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–D.

claim: Reduced dlg1 expression led to loss of wing margin and sensory bristles in the adult wing blade.
source: Furthermore, we demonstrated that reduced dlg1 expression led to accumulation of extracellular Wg (Figure 4C,D), attenuation of Wg signaling in wing discs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–D), and consequently loss of wing margin and sensory bristles in the adult wing blade (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by adult wing phenotype data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E.

claim: Overexpressed dlg1 was sufficient to rescue wing margin defects caused by dysfunctional pre-EJC.
source: Significantly, overexpressed dlg1 was sufficient to rescue wing margin defects caused by dysfunctional pre-EJC (Figure 4—figure supplement 3H).
evidence: This is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3H.

claim: Inhibiting Rnps1 in the wing disc resulted in defects in Dlg1 protein production.
source: It is known that additional splicing factors are required for the pre-EJC activity (Reichert et al., 2002). Inhibiting one of such factors, Rnps1, in the wing disc resulted in the same defect in Dlg1 and Dsh protein production as well as Wg signaling activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inhibiting Rnps1 in the wing disc resulted in defects in Dsh protein production.
source: It is known that additional splicing factors are required for the pre-EJC activity (Reichert et al., 2002). Inhibiting one of such factors, Rnps1, in the wing disc resulted in the same defect in Dlg1 and Dsh protein production as well as Wg signaling activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Inhibiting Rnps1 in the wing disc resulted in defects in Wg signaling activation.
source: It is known that additional splicing factors are required for the pre-EJC activity (Reichert et al., 2002). Inhibiting one of such factors, Rnps1, in the wing disc resulted in the same defect in Dlg1 and Dsh protein production as well as Wg signaling activation (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The pre-EJC mediated splicing activity positively regulates dlg1 to control Wg signaling in Drosophila.
source: Together, these experiments indicate that the pre-EJC mediated splicing activity positively regulates dlg1 to control Wg signaling in Drosophila.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined genetic and molecular data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dlg1 is important for the maintenance of cell polarity.
source: Dlg1 is important for the maintenance of cell polarity, acting together with L(2)gl to form a basolateral complex to counteract with the apical complex in epithelium (St Johnston and Ahringer, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dlg1 acts together with L(2)gl to form a basolateral complex to counteract with the apical complex in epithelium.
source: Dlg1 is important for the maintenance of cell polarity, acting together with L(2)gl to form a basolateral complex to counteract with the apical complex in epithelium (St Johnston and Ahringer, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Reduced pre-EJC activity led to altered cell polarity in wing disc epithelium.
source: Therefore, it is not surprising that reduced pre-EJC activity led to altered cell polarity in wing disc epithelium (Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claim: Loss of L(2)gl in wing disc clones did not obviously affect Wg signaling.
source: To investigate if the maintenance of cell polarity is required for Wg signaling, we examined the effects of L(2)gl as well as Bazooka (Baz) and Cdc42 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), two apical complex members (Harris and Peifer, 2004; Warner and Longmore, 2009), in the Wg signal transduction. Surprisingly, loss of these polarity regulators in wing disc clones did not obviously affect Wg signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), implying that the regulation of Wg signaling by Dlg1 may be independent of its function on cell polarity.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of Baz in wing disc clones did not obviously affect Wg signaling.
source: To investigate if the maintenance of cell polarity is required for Wg signaling, we examined the effects of L(2)gl as well as Bazooka (Baz) and Cdc42 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), two apical complex members (Harris and Peifer, 2004; Warner and Longmore, 2009), in the Wg signal transduction. Surprisingly, loss of these polarity regulators in wing disc clones did not obviously affect Wg signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), implying that the regulation of Wg signaling by Dlg1 may be independent of its function on cell polarity.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Loss of Cdc42 in wing disc clones did not obviously affect Wg signaling.
source: To investigate if the maintenance of cell polarity is required for Wg signaling, we examined the effects of L(2)gl as well as Bazooka (Baz) and Cdc42 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), two apical complex members (Harris and Peifer, 2004; Warner and Longmore, 2009), in the Wg signal transduction. Surprisingly, loss of these polarity regulators in wing disc clones did not obviously affect Wg signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), implying that the regulation of Wg signaling by Dlg1 may be independent of its function on cell polarity.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The regulation of Wg signaling by Dlg1 may be independent of its function on cell polarity.
source: To investigate if the maintenance of cell polarity is required for Wg signaling, we examined the effects of L(2)gl as well as Bazooka (Baz) and Cdc42 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), two apical complex members (Harris and Peifer, 2004; Warner and Longmore, 2009), in the Wg signal transduction. Surprisingly, loss of these polarity regulators in wing disc clones did not obviously affect Wg signaling (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), implying that the regulation of Wg signaling by Dlg1 may be independent of its function on cell polarity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that other polarity regulators do not affect Wg signaling.

claim: Drosophila Dsh binds in vitro to the K-K-x-x-x-Ψ motif within the I3-insert of the Hook domain in Dlg1.
source: It has been reported that Drosophila Dsh binds in vitro to the K-K-x-x-x-Ψ motif within the I3-insert of the Hook domain in Dlg1 (Garcia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dsh interacts with Dlg1 in S2 cells.
source: We confirmed this interaction in S2 cells as well as in wing discs by immunoprecipitation (Figure 4G,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Dsh interacts with Dlg1 in wing discs.
source: We confirmed this interaction in S2 cells as well as in wing discs by immunoprecipitation (Figure 4G,H; Figure 4—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Overexpressed dsh was able to largely rescue the wing margin defects associated with reduced dlg1 activity.
source: The relevance of such interaction was further illustrated in rescue experiments in which overexpressed dsh was able to largely rescue the wing margin defects associated with reduced dlg1 activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This is supported by genetic rescue data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3G.

claim: Knocking down dlg1 by RNAi in S2 cells led to reduced production of Dsh protein.
source: Knocking down dlg1 by RNAi in S2 cells led to reduced production of Dsh protein, whilst overexpressing dlg1 had an opposite effect (Figure 5A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Overexpressing dlg1 in S2 cells increased the production of Dsh protein.
source: Knocking down dlg1 by RNAi in S2 cells led to reduced production of Dsh protein, whilst overexpressing dlg1 had an opposite effect (Figure 5A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 4—figure supplement 5C.

claim: Knocking down dlg1 in wing discs reduced the amount of Dsh protein.
source: A similar result was observed in vivo when dlg1 expression was manipulated in wing discs (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Overexpressing dlg1 in wing discs increased the amount of Dsh protein.
source: A similar result was observed in vivo when dlg1 expression was manipulated in wing discs (Figure 5C–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: Dsh protein ectopically produced in S2 cells exhibited a short half-life of around two hours.
source: Dsh protein ectopically produced in S2 cells exhibited a short half-life of around two hours (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The degradation of Dsh protein occurred mainly in lysosome when nascent protein synthesis was blocked by cycloheximide (CHX).
source: We found that the degradation of Dsh protein occurred mainly in lysosome when nascent protein synthesis was blocked by cycloheximide (CHX) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by drug treatment data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Dsh colocalized with early endosome markers in wing discs.
source: This is consistent with the observation that Dsh colocalized with early endosome and late endosome/lysosome markers in wing discs as well as in S2 cells (Figure 5H–M; Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 5H–J.

claim: Dsh colocalized with late endosome/lysosome markers in wing discs.
source: This is consistent with the observation that Dsh colocalized with early endosome and late endosome/lysosome markers in wing discs as well as in S2 cells (Figure 5H–M; Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 5K–M.

claim: Dsh colocalized with early endosome markers in S2 cells.
source: This is consistent with the observation that Dsh colocalized with early endosome and late endosome/lysosome markers in wing discs as well as in S2 cells (Figure 5H–M; Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Dsh colocalized with late endosome/lysosome markers in S2 cells.
source: This is consistent with the observation that Dsh colocalized with early endosome and late endosome/lysosome markers in wing discs as well as in S2 cells (Figure 5H–M; Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Heightened dlg1 expression counteracted with the CHX effect on Dsh degradation.
source: Furthermore, heightened dlg1 expression counteracted with the CHX effect on Dsh degradation (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Dsh degradation potentiated by tsu RNAi could be prevented when S2 cells were treated with chloroquine (CQ).
source: In contrast, Dsh degradation potentiated by tsu or dlg1 RNAi could be prevented when S2 cells were treated with a lysosomal inhibitor chloroquine (CQ) (Figure 5O,P).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5O.

claim: Dsh degradation potentiated by dlg1 RNAi could be prevented when S2 cells were treated with chloroquine (CQ).
source: In contrast, Dsh degradation potentiated by tsu or dlg1 RNAi could be prevented when S2 cells were treated with a lysosomal inhibitor chloroquine (CQ) (Figure 5O,P).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5P.

claim: The interaction between Dlg1 and Dsh protects Dsh protein from degradation in the lysosome.
source: The above data indicate that the interaction between Dlg1 and Dsh protects Dsh protein from degradation in the lysosome.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined data on Dlg1-Dsh interaction and Dsh degradation.

claim: Increased dlg1 expression correlated with reduced degree of ubiquitination modification on Dsh.
source: This conclusion was supported further by the observation that increased dlg1 expression correlated with reduced degree of ubiquitination modification on Dsh, a form of posttranslational modifications required for protein degradation (Figure 5Q).
evidence: This is supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5Q.

claim: Regulated protein degradation serves as a control mechanism on Dvl protein homeostasis in cultured vertebrate cells.
source: Consistent with a role of Dlg1 on Dsh stability in Drosophila wing development, regulated protein degradation serves as a control mechanism on Dvl protein homeostasis in cultured vertebrate cells (Gao and Chen, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Human cells encode five orthologous Dlg proteins, Dlg1-5.
source: Human cells encode five orthologous Dlg proteins, Dlg1-5.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about human Dlg proteins.

claim: Only Dlg2 contains an intact K-K-x-x-x-Ψ motif required for Dsh interaction.
source: However, only Dlg2 contains an intact K-K-x-x-x-Ψ motif required for Dsh interaction as elucidated in Drosophila (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overproduced Dlg2 was sufficient to stabilize Dvl proteins in HEK293T cells.
source: Indeed, overproduced Dlg2, but not Dlg3, was sufficient to stabilize Dvl proteins in HEK293T cells (Figure 6B,E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overproduced Dlg3 was not sufficient to stabilize Dvl proteins in HEK293T cells.
source: Indeed, overproduced Dlg2, but not Dlg3, was sufficient to stabilize Dvl proteins in HEK293T cells (Figure 6B,E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The Dlg2KKAA mutant failed to stabilize Dvl.
source: As predicted, this Dlg2 mutant failed to stabilize Dvl due to its inability to interact with Dvl (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The Dlg2KKAA mutant is unable to interact with Dvl.
source: As predicted, this Dlg2 mutant failed to stabilize Dvl due to its inability to interact with Dvl (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The Dlg2SFI-NL mutant showed reduced interaction with Dvl.
source: The resulting Dlg2SFI-NL mutant showed reduced interaction with Dvl and no effect on Dvl protein stabilization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The Dlg2SFI-NL mutant had no effect on Dvl protein stabilization.
source: The resulting Dlg2SFI-NL mutant showed reduced interaction with Dvl and no effect on Dvl protein stabilization (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Overexpressed wildtype dlg2 enhanced the Dvl-induced TOPFlash reporter activity.
source: To further demonstrate functional consequence of Dlg2 regulation on Dvl protein stability in Wnt signaling, we performed TOPFlash Luciferase Wnt signaling reporter assay in HEK293T cells. Overexpressed wildtype but not the KKAA mutant form of dlg2 enhanced further the Dvl-induced TOPFlash reporter activity (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by TOPFlash reporter assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The KKAA mutant form of dlg2 did not enhance the Dvl-induced TOPFlash reporter activity.
source: To further demonstrate functional consequence of Dlg2 regulation on Dvl protein stability in Wnt signaling, we performed TOPFlash Luciferase Wnt signaling reporter assay in HEK293T cells. Overexpressed wildtype but not the KKAA mutant form of dlg2 enhanced further the Dvl-induced TOPFlash reporter activity (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by TOPFlash reporter assay data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The Dlg activity on Dvl protein homeostasis is conserved from flies to vertebrates.
source: The above experiments together indicate that the Dlg activity on Dvl protein homeostasis is conserved from flies to vertebrates.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both Drosophila and human Dlg proteins regulate Dsh/Dvl stability.

claim: The EJC activity is indispensable for Wg signaling by maintaining an appropriate level of Dsh protein for Wg ligand reception in Drosophila.
source: Our genetic and biochemical analyses demonstrate that the pre-EJC is necessary for Wg morphogen reception to activate the signal transduction.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the primary findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: The identification of dlg1 as one of the pre-EJC targets provides mechanistic basis for the pre-EJC regulation of the Wg signaling.
source: The identification of the cell polarity determinant dlg1 as one of the pre-EJC targets provides mechanistic basis for the pre-EJC regulation of the Wg signaling.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings supported by the experimental data.

claim: Dlg1 protein controls the stability of the scaffold protein Dsh, which is the hub of the Wg signaling cascade.
source: Dlg1 controls the stability of the scaffold protein Dsh, which is the hub of the Wg signaling cascade (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings supported by the experimental data and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: The mode of regulation of Dvl by Dlg is conserved from flies to vertebrates.
source: Importantly, this mode of regulation of Dvl by Dlg is conserved from flies to vertebrates.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings supported by the experimental data in both Drosophila and human cells.

claim: The EJC as well as other RNA binding protein complexes are thought to function in a pleiotropic manner.
source: The EJC as well as other RNA binding protein complexes are thought to function in a pleiotropic manner.
evidence: This is a statement of prevailing scientific understanding.

claim: RNA regulatory machineries can act specifically on developmental signaling for pattern formation and organogenesis.
source: However, our data presented here together with several recent studies argue that RNA regulatory machineries can act specifically on developmental signaling for pattern formation and organogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the findings of this study and recent literature.

claim: Apical localization of wg RNA is essential for signal activation in epithelial cells.
source: It has been increasingly recognized that the production, transport or the location of mRNA are subject to precise regulation in Wg/Wnt signaling. For example, apical localization of wg RNA is essential for signal activation in epithelial cells (Simmonds et al., 2001; Wilkie and Davis, 2001), whilst the RNA binding protein RBM47 regulates Wnt signaling in zebrafish head development (Guan et al., 2013) as well as in cancer (Vanharanta et al., 2014; Venugopal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The RNA binding protein RBM47 regulates Wnt signaling in zebrafish head development.
source: It has been increasingly recognized that the production, transport or the location of mRNA are subject to precise regulation in Wg/Wnt signaling. For example, apical localization of wg RNA is essential for signal activation in epithelial cells (Simmonds et al., 2001; Wilkie and Davis, 2001), whilst the RNA binding protein RBM47 regulates Wnt signaling in zebrafish head development (Guan et al., 2013) as well as in cancer (Vanharanta et al., 2014; Venugopal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The RNA binding protein RBM47 regulates Wnt signaling in cancer.
source: It has been increasingly recognized that the production, transport or the location of mRNA are subject to precise regulation in Wg/Wnt signaling. For example, apical localization of wg RNA is essential for signal activation in epithelial cells (Simmonds et al., 2001; Wilkie and Davis, 2001), whilst the RNA binding protein RBM47 regulates Wnt signaling in zebrafish head development (Guan et al., 2013) as well as in cancer (Vanharanta et al., 2014; Venugopal et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RNA binding protein Quaking specifically binds to the 3'UTR of transcription factor gli2a mRNA to modulate Hedgehog signaling in zebrafish muscle development.
source: It has been reported that RNA-binding protein Quaking specifically binds to the 3'UTR of transcription factor gli2a mRNA to modulate Hedgehog signaling in zebrafish muscle development (Lobbardi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: RNA binding protein RBM5/6 and 10 could differentially control alternative splicing of a negative Notch regulator gene NUMB.
source: RNA binding protein RBM5/6 and 10 could differentially control alternative splicing of a negative Notch regulator gene NUMB, thus antagonistically regulating the Notch signaling activity for cancer cell proliferation (Bechara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The most studied function of the EJC in development is to localize oskar mRNA to the posterior pole of the oocyte for oocyte polarity establishment and germ cell formation in Drosophila.
source: The most studied function of the EJC in development is to localize oskar mRNA to the posterior pole of the oocyte for oocyte polarity establishment and germ cell formation in Drosophila (Newmark and Boswell, 1994; Hachet and Ephrussi, 2001; Mohr et al., 2001; van Eeden et al., 2001; Palacios et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proper oskar RNA localization relies on its mRNA splicing.
source: Further study suggests that the proper oskar RNA localization relies on its mRNA splicing (Hachet and Ephrussi, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EJC might regulate oskar mRNA splicing to mediate its mRNA localization.
source: In light of our study of the EJC activity on dlg1 mRNA as well as the roles of EJC on mapk and piwi splicing (Ashton-Beaucage et al., 2010; Roignant and Treisman, 2010; Hayashi et al., 2014; Malone et al., 2014), we suspect that EJC might regulate oskar mRNA splicing to mediate its mRNA localization.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of this study and previous literature.

claim: EJC may primarily regulate Wg and MAPK signaling in patterning the developing wing.
source: Apart from defects in Wg and MAPK signaling, however, we did not observe altered wing patterning associated with other developmental signaling systems in EJC defective flies, arguing that EJC may primarily regulate Wg and MAPK signaling in patterning the developing wing.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only Wg and MAPK signaling defects were observed in EJC mutants.

claim: Polarized localization of Fz and Fz2 proteins is essential for activation of non-canonical and canonical Wg signaling, respectively.
source: In Drosophila, polarized localization of Fz and Fz2 proteins is essential for activation of non-canonical and canonical Wg signaling, respectively (Boutros et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dsh is found at both the apical cell boundary and in the basal side of the cytoplasm.
source: Dsh, which acts as a hub mediating both canonical and non-canonical Wg signaling, however, is found at both the apical cell boundary and in the basal side of the cytoplasm (Kaplan and Tolwinski, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The polarized activity of Dsh must require distinct regulatory mechanisms at different sub-membrane compartments.
source: Thus, the polarized activity of Dsh must require distinct regulatory mechanisms at different sub-membrane compartments (Mlodzik, 2016).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of Dsh localization and supported by citation.

claim: The basolateral polarity determinant Dlg1 may play a dominant role to control the Dsh abundance/activity in canonical Wg signaling.
source: Our results provide the in vivo evidence suggesting that the basolateral polarity determinant Dlg1 may play a dominant role to control the Dsh abundance/activity in canonical Wg signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings of this study.

claim: Altered Dvl production or activity has been linked with several forms of cancer.
source: Altered Dvl production or activity has been linked with several forms of cancer (Kafka et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The stability of Dvl proteins can be controlled through regulated protein degradation both in vertebrates and in Drosophila.
source: The stability of Dvl proteins can be controlled through regulated protein degradation both in vertebrates (Gao and Chen, 2010) and in Drosophila as reported in this study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and the findings of this study.

claim: In HEK293T cells, Dapper1 induces autophagic degradation of Dvl2 in lysosome.
source: In HEK293T cells, Dapper1 induces whilst Myc-interacting zinc-finger protein 1 (MIZ1) antagonizes autophagic degradation of Dvl2 in lysosome (Zhang et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In HEK293T cells, Myc-interacting zinc-finger protein 1 (MIZ1) antagonizes autophagic degradation of Dvl2 in lysosome.
source: In HEK293T cells, Dapper1 induces whilst Myc-interacting zinc-finger protein 1 (MIZ1) antagonizes autophagic degradation of Dvl2 in lysosome (Zhang et al., 2006; Huang et al., 2015; Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A tumor suppressor CYLD deubiquitinase inhibits the ubiquitination of Dvl.
source: It is also reported that a tumor suppressor CYLD deubiquitinase inhibits the ubiquitination of Dvl (Tauriello et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Upregulation of dvl2 expression has been found in various forms of cancer.
source: Furthermore, upregulation of dvl2 and dlg2 expression has been found in various forms of cancer as shown in the COSMIC database (Forbes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a database.

claim: Upregulation of dlg2 expression has been found in various forms of cancer.
source: Furthermore, upregulation of dvl2 and dlg2 expression has been found in various forms of cancer as shown in the COSMIC database (Forbes et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a database.

claim: Dsh is known to interact with L(2)gl.
source: Dsh is known to interact with L(2)gl.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: Dsh activity is required for correct localization of L(2)gl to establish apical-basal polarity in Xenopus ectoderm and Drosophila follicular epithelium.
source: On one hand, Dsh activity is required for correct localization of L(2)gl to establish apical-basal polarity in Xenopus ectoderm and Drosophila follicular epithelium (Dollar et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: L(2)gl can regulate Dsh to maintain planar organization of the embryonic epidermis in Drosophila.
source: On the other hand, L(2)gl can regulate Dsh to maintain planar organization of the embryonic epidermis in Drosophila (Kaplan and Tolwinski, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Dsh binds to Dlg1 to activate Guk Holder-dependent spindle positioning in Drosophila.
source: A recent report suggests that Dsh binds to Dlg1 to activate Guk Holder-dependent spindle positioning in Drosophila (Garcia et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The interactions among Dsh, Dlg1 and L(2)gl may be dependent on their localization.
source: It is likely that the interactions among Dsh, Dlg1 and L(2)gl may be dependent on their localization, and Dsh may serve as a bridge to connect cell signaling and polarity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and known protein localizations.

claim: Dsh may serve as a bridge to connect cell signaling and polarity.
source: It is likely that the interactions among Dsh, Dlg1 and L(2)gl may be dependent on their localization, and Dsh may serve as a bridge to connect cell signaling and polarity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings and known protein functions.

claim: Non-canonical Wg/Wnt signaling acts through cytoskeletal regulators to establish planar cell polarity.
source: It is well known that Wg/Wnt signaling controls cell polarity in distinct manner. Non-canonical signaling acts through cytoskeletal regulators to establish planar cell polarity (Yang and Mlodzik, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Canonical Wg/Wnt signaling may directly affect apical-basal cell polarity.
source: Canonical signaling may also directly affect apical-basal cell polarity (Karner et al., 2006).
